<div>

![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image}

The First Law of Geography is that "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" Waldo Tobler. Quantitatively, this can be expressed as **spatial autocorrelation** -- the correlation of values in a variable by distance. Put in the context of Tobler's First Law of Geography, we might expect that values associated with spatial objects that are close to one another are more similar than those that are further apart. Of course, the distance in which values are correlated will depend on the variable you are studying. In this video lesson (runtime: 49:28) we will explore the all-important concept of spatial autocorrelation (see the classic paper "[Spatial Autocorrelation: Trouble or New Paradigm?](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/1939924){target="blank"}"; Legendre 1993) and how to address it in your data. Specifically, we will cover:

* What spatial autocorrelation is
* How to detect spatial autocorrelation in a sample
* How to *avoid* spatial autocorrelation in you study design
* How to test for spatial autocorrelation in your model results
* How to *use* spatial autocorrelation!

*Note: Much of this video lesson is quite complex and you will not be evaluated on most of the material herein. Material that you will be evaluated on includes purrr's `keep()` function, `terra::ext()`, and `terra::aggregate()`.*

</div>

## Addendum: A closer look at raster aggregation

We used `terra::aggregate()` in the video above to change a raster to a coarser resolution. Unfortunately,  I did a very bad job of explaining how to do so. As such, I decided to provide a bit more explanation.

Let's set up a new session for a quick exploration of `terra::aggregate()`:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(tidyverse)

# Set tmap to "view" for the entire session:

tmap_mode("view")

# Read in the digital elevation model raster data:

dem <- 
  terra::rast("data/raw/rasters/dem_dc_10m.tif")

# Read in dc_land:

dc_land <-
  st_read(
    "data/raw/shapefiles/dc_land.geojson", 
    quiet = TRUE
  )
```

For our example, I will use `terra::spatSample()` to generate 5,000 random point samples within the spatial extent of `dem` and convert the points to *sf* files:

```{r}
rando_points <- 
  dem %>% 
  terra::spatSample(
    size = 5000,
    method = "random",
    as.points = TRUE,
    values = FALSE,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  st_as_sf()
```

Let's have a look at our point and raster data on a map:

```{r}
# Add the elevation model:

dem %>% 
  tm_shape(name = "Elevation") +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale =
      tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)),
    col.legend =
      tm_legend(title = "Elevation")
  ) +
  
  # Add random points:
  
  rando_points %>% 
  tm_shape(name = "Rando points") +
  tm_dots()
```

You will notice that the we received the warning message "stars object downsampled to ...". We have seen that warning message a lot. It means that the raster has been modified to a courser resolution. Rather than letting *tmap* modify our resolution for us, we can do so directly with `terra::aggregate()`. We supply (at a minimum):

* `x = ...`: The target raster;
* `fact = ...`: An integer value specifying the number of cells in each direction to aggregate (*Note: There are other options, but I rarely use them*);
* `fun = ...`: The function used to aggregate the values (i.e., since the cells have different values, we need to know how to combine those values for the new raster cells).

In the code below, I aggregate `dem` by a factor of 4 and use the function `mean` to combine the values:

```{r}
dem_agg <-
  dem %>% 
  terra::aggregate(
    fact = 4,
    fun = "mean",
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
```

Let's look at the metadata of the two rasters to compare the original and aggregated cell sizes:

```{r}
dem

dem_agg
```

We can see that the resolution of the original raster was about 9.2 meters whereas the resolution of the aggregated raster is almost 37 meters!

Moreover, our new raster has considerably fewer cells, so we can now plot data without a warning message:

```{r}
# Add the elevation model:

dem_agg %>% 
  tm_shape(name = "Elevation") +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale =
      tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)),
    col.legend =
      tm_legend(title = "Elevation")
  ) +
  
  # Add random points:
  
  rando_points %>% 
  tm_shape(name = "Rando points") +
  tm_dots()
```

This operation can also be analytically useful. For example, perhaps we might want to count the number of observations per raster cell -- in doing so, the resolution of cells can really make a difference. We can use `terra::rasterize()` to do so. Below, let's count the number of sampling points per raster cell (`fun = "length"`) using the original ~10m resolution digital elevation model:

```{r}
# Rasterize the points to the original dem raster:

rando_points %>% 
  terra::rasterize(
    y = dem,
    fun = "length",
    background = 0
  ) %>% 
  
  # Mask the resultant raster:
  
  terra::mask(dc_land) %>% 
  
  # Plot the data:
  
  tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(),
    col.legend =
      tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell")
  )
```

We can see from the legend that there are some values that are not zero, but you really have to zoom in to see those locations. Additionally, the maximum value is "1" suggesting that there is no more than one point per cell.

We can improve this a little bit by using an aggregated raster:

```{r}
# Rasterize the points to the aggregated dem raster:

rando_points %>% 
  terra::rasterize(
    y = dem_agg,
    fun = "length",
    background = 0
  ) %>% 
  
  # Mask the resultant raster:
  
  terra::mask(dc_land) %>% 
  
  # Plot the data:
  
  tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(),
    col.legend =
      tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell")
  )
```

But the level of improvement is minimal -- there are now more points per raster cell, however points are still rather difficult to observe. We can improve this by aggregating the data even further. I like to aim towards a target resolution that might make sense. 

For example, perhaps my goal is to determine the number of samples per square kilometer (1 km^2^ is 1000 x 1000m). I can use the resolution of the current raster cells to determine how many cells I need to aggregate. We can use `terra::res()` to return a vector with the x and y resolution of a raster:

```{r}
terra::res(dem)
```

We can then (roughly) determine the number of cells that need to be aggregated to achieve that resolution:

```{r}
1000 / terra::res(dem)[[1]]
```

*Note: Because the x and y values of the resolution are equivalent, I use `[[...]]` to extract just one of the values.*

Rounding this, we can see that we need to aggregate the data by a factor of `109` to generate raster cells of roughly 1 km^2^.

Below, I rasterize based on the original raster with `fun = "length"` and then aggregate the resultant data with `fact = 109` (109 cells in the horizontal and vertical dimensions) and `fun = "sum"`:

```{r}

# Rasterize the points to the original dem raster:

rando_points %>% 
  terra::rasterize(
    y = dem,
    fun = "length",
    background = 0
  ) %>% 
  
  # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell
  # (at a course resolution):
  
  terra::aggregate(
    fact = 109,
    fun = "sum",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  
  # Mask the resultant raster:

  terra::mask(dc_land) %>% 
  
  # Plot the data:
  
  tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(),
    col.legend =
      tm_legend(title = "Points per square kilometer")
  )
```

Be sure to use the metadata to check the new resolution of the aggregated raster:

```{r}
# Rasterize the points to the original dem raster:

rando_points %>% 
  terra::rasterize(
    y = dem,
    fun = "length",
    background = 0
  ) %>% 
  
  # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell
  # (at a course resolution):
  
  terra::aggregate(
    fact = 109,
    fun = "sum",
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
```

<button class="accordion">Metacharacters in regex</button>
::: panel

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Metacharacters are not R functions!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

When you are given a list of functions that you may use in a given problem set, recall that regex metacharacters are not functions. As such, they will not be included in your function list. You may use *any* metacharacter to address a given problem!
:::

* **Alternation constraint**, `(...)`: Constrains the use of a metacharacter to just the symbols inside of parentheses
* **Anchor**, `^...`: Specify the start of a string
* **Anchor**, `...$`: Specify the end of a string
* **Character class**, `[...]`: Define a *set* of symbols that you would like to match
* **Metacharacter escape**, `\\`: Treat a metacharacter as a literal character
* **Optional match**, `?`: Specify that the preceding symbol is optional
* **Range** (in a character class), `[...-...]`: Define a *range* of symbols that you would like to match in a given position
* **Or**, `...|...`: Specify a match of one string "or" another string
* **Repetition**, `...*`: Specify that a symbol can appear no times or an unlimited number of times
* **Repetition**, `...+`: Specify that a symbol appears at least once or an unlimited number of times
* **Repetition**, `{...}`: Specify the number of times a symbol should appear
* **Repetition**, `{...,...}`: Specify that a symbol may appear within a range of repetitions
* **Wild card**, `.`: Specify that a character value at a given location can be any symbol
:::
